en.title: APA, IEEE and Harvard citation guide
en.body:
The templates below are fictional teaching examples, not published references. Replace every placeholder with verified source information.

APA (7th edition - summary)

Journal article reference:

Author, A. (Year). Title of article. Journal Title, volume(issue), pages. https://doi.org/xxxx

IEEE

In-text citations are numeric [1] and the reference list is numbered:

[1] A. Author, "Title of paper," Journal, vol., no., pp., year.

Harvard

Author-date system: (Author, Year) — references listed alphabetically.

Accurate citations from discovery to reference list

Follow the institution or journal’s chosen style. Verify author, year, title and identifier against the original source. Harvard has institution-specific variants. Never add fabricated or unverified references.

  • Cross-check in-text citations and the reference list
  • Verify DOI and bibliographic details at the source
  • Record page numbers for quotations where required
  • Review Zotero or EndNote output before delivery

Reference management without hidden errors

Create one project reference library and merge duplicates. Connect PDFs and notes to the correct record. Imported metadata may be incomplete; verify title, authors and year with the publisher.

Cite what you actually consulted

If the original source is inaccessible, use your style’s secondary-citation rules rather than implying you reviewed it. Ideas, data, figures and code can need attribution, not just direct wording. Check reuse licenses and permission for figures separately.

Final review

  • Every citation points to the correct record.
  • Removed references do not linger in the list.
  • The final style follows current institutional guidance.
  • DOIs, URLs and punctuation are checked.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Do not transfer an imported search record directly into the final paper. In this exercise a record has a wrong year and an incomplete author list: compare the publisher or original document with its title and DOI, then correct the metadata. If you only read a secondary source, use the style’s permitted secondary-citation approach. A valid DOI attached to a different title is still wrong. Check quotation location and figure permissions separately. Names in the format examples above are fictional.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
DiscoveryImported record with incomplete metadataHas the original been found?
CorrectionTitle, authors, year and DOIDo all identify one document?
CitationRequired outlet styleAre quotations and paraphrases distinct?
ReconciliationText versus reference listAny orphan entries or citations?
RightsAdapted figure and separate licenceIs permission and credit adequate?

Exercise output: Create a corrected reference library and text/list reconciliation record.
en.desc: Review educational citation templates, reconcile in-text citations and reference lists, check DOI records and follow your institution’s style guidance.
outcomes: Create a corrected reference library and text/list reconciliation record.

en.title: Interpreting Turnitin and iThenticate similarity
en.body:
Practical procedures for using similarity-check tools and interpreting results, plus methods to reduce non-permitted similarity.

Turnitin vs iThenticate

Key differences: Turnitin is widely used in academic coursework contexts, while iThenticate is designed for manuscripts and publication screening. Tips on uploading, limits and result analysis.

Interpreting similarity reports

The report should include overall percentage, matched sources list, highlighted segments and annotation about the type of match (quoted text, common phrases, prior self-publication).

Reduction strategies and rewriting

Patterns for rewriting, correct referencing, paraphrasing strategies and documentation to reduce similarity percentage.

Similarity requires human interpretation

Scores depend on settings, matching databases and document length. Correct quotations, references and common phrases may match. The aim is accurate attribution and original scholarly expression, not hiding matches or targeting an arbitrary percentage. No automated tool guarantees complete originality.

  • Record tool, date and report settings
  • Distinguish valid quotations from unattributed reuse
  • Cite original sources and improve the argument structure
  • Respect confidentiality when uploading manuscripts

A scholarly revision workflow

Identify whether a match comes from references, common language, a valid quotation or unattributed reuse. For unattributed ideas, swapping a few words is insufficient: express your understanding and cite the source. Retain exact language only with appropriate quotation and citation.

Why settings matter

Excluding references or quotations, setting minimum match size and selecting comparison databases may change the score. Compare versions with equivalent settings. Translation and database limitations affect coverage. A low score does not rule out fabricated references, invented data or weak reasoning.

Before uploading confidential manuscripts, check authorization and service retention policy. Commercial tool access must be lawful and agreed. This website itself is not Turnitin or iThenticate.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Read a similarity report to assess attribution and wording, not to find a magic percentage. In the fictional case, references and correctly attributed quotations raise the score, while one unattributed paragraph also appears among matches. Record settings, the submitted version and the source of each match. Database coverage, translation and unindexed material can hide issues. Changing words merely to reduce a percentage does not repair idea attribution or authorship problems.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
InputFixed text version and settingsIs the submission recorded?
Legitimate matchReference title or attributed quoteIs attribution correct?
Problem matchUnattributed paragraphWere wording and idea origins examined?
CorrectionUnderstood paraphrase and citationIs it more than word substitution?
ReviewMatches and action logDoes it meet the outlet policy?

Exercise output: Produce a match-by-match interpretation and documented correction record.
en.desc: Understand textual matches, quotations, citations and report settings. Learn the limits of similarity scores and a responsible approach to revision.
worksheet: Were wording and idea origins examined?
Is it more than word substitution?
Does it meet the outlet policy?
outcomes: Produce a match-by-match interpretation and documented correction record.

en.title: Similarity reports: components and revision checklist
en.body:
A comprehensive report must include the following sections:

  1. Executive summary — overall similarity percentage and recommended action
  2. Details of each matched source with reference/link
  3. Highlighted matching text with location/page references
  4. Recommended corrective actions and next steps
  5. Final assessment and recommendation for publication or revision

A reviewable report goes beyond a score

Identify the location, source and proposed action for each concern. Document version and date matter: an earlier report does not describe a revised manuscript. Do not declare misconduct solely from a percentage.

  • Document version and tool details
  • Matching table with location, source and use category
  • Prioritized revision plan with responsibilities
  • Human review against institutional policy

An example revision-action table

LocationIssueAction
Specified page and paragraphUnattributed ideaIndependent expression and original citation
Direct quotationMissing marks or pageComplete under the chosen style
Standard methodMatching technical phraseHuman contextual assessment
Reference listBibliographic matchRecord settings and verify the reference

This is an educational example, not a completed report on your manuscript. Distinguish attribution problems, explainable similarity and issues requiring institutional judgment. A reviewer should not decide misconduct only from a tool’s color or score. Retain filename, version and date to track revisions.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Two documents with the same percentage may have different problems. In fictional A, most matches are technical terms and references; in B, a complete unattributed argument appears. A useful summary describes match types and actions rather than declaring misconduct from the aggregate score. Any secondary view excluding references or quotations needs transparent settings and should not conceal the original report. The actual text, provenance, attribution and institutional policy determine the decision.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
ReportVersion, date and settingsComparable with the earlier report?
ClassificationQuote, reference, wording or ideaHas each source been examined?
InterpretationA and B with similar percentagesIs judgment tied to the text?
ActionCite, quote, rewrite or seek adviceIs the reason recorded?
ApprovalAuthor review and local policyIs the tool report distinguished from a decision?

Exercise output: Keep a match/reason/action matrix with the original report.
en.desc: Review report components, document versions and tool settings, and use a revision-action table. A similarity percentage alone cannot determine plagiarism.
worksheet: A and B with similar percentages
Is judgment tied to the text?
Cite, quote, rewrite or seek advice
Is the tool report distinguished from a decision?
outcomes: Keep a match/reason/action matrix with the original report.

en.title: Scientific article types and journal selection
en.body:
Explanation of article types, acceptance criteria, typical structure and submission tips for ISI-indexed and non-ISI journals.

  • Original Research: Papers that present new empirical findings and data.
  • Review Article: Systematic or narrative reviews summarizing existing knowledge.
  • Conference Paper: Shorter reports or preliminary findings presented at conferences.
  • Short Communication / Case Study: Small focused reports or specific case descriptions.

Journal selection and submission readiness

ISI is not an article type. Select the article category from the journal’s author guidelines. Verify scope, data requirements, authorship policy, publication charges and indexing using original sources. Acceptance and review turnaround cannot be guaranteed.

  • Structure the manuscript around study and article type
  • Use appropriate reporting guidance, such as PRISMA or CONSORT
  • Prepare contribution, conflict-of-interest and data statements
  • Respond respectfully and point by point to reviewers

Build an article around one central message

Converting a dissertation into an article is more than shortening chapters. Select a question and central message, retain supporting evidence and adapt the writing to the journal audience. Simultaneous submission or undisclosed duplicate publication may breach publishing policies.

Abstract and discussion

Keep the abstract consistent with actual findings; do not claim more certainty than the evidence supports. Compare relevant studies, consider alternative explanations and describe how limitations affect interpretation. Practical recommendations need evidential support.

Before submission

  • All authors approved the version.
  • Numbers and units match between text and tables.
  • Ethics, funding, conflict and data statements are complete.
  • References, title, abstract and keywords were checked.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Practice consistent reporting across the abstract, methods and discussion of an observational finding. The abstract should not claim a causal effect when the design estimates association. Specify sample, units, estimator and uncertainty, and never insert fictional values as actual results. Use a question/evidence map to remove repetition and unsupported conclusions. Abstract limits and article structure follow the outlet. Before submission, authors verify numbers, references and disclosures of tool assistance.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
AbstractAim, design, actual finding and limitConsistent with the paper?
MethodsSample, instruments, analysis and changesAssessable and reproducible?
ResultsEstimate and interval with unitsAre required findings included?
DiscussionAlternatives and scopeWithin the design’s support?
SubmissionRights, references and author approvalAre relevant policies checked?

Exercise output: Prepare a coherent draft and claim-to-evidence matrix.
en.desc: Understand original research, review articles and other formats, plan a manuscript and prepare submission. Distinguish journal indexing from article type.
worksheet: Aim, design, actual finding and limit
outcomes: Prepare a coherent draft and claim-to-evidence matrix.

en.title: Systematic reviews and PRISMA: a practical workflow
en.desc: Plan a review protocol, reproducible search, screening, evidence extraction and PRISMA reporting. Keep reporting quality distinct from study validity.
en.body:
Question and protocol

Where appropriate, define population, intervention or exposure, comparison and outcome. Specify eligibility, sources, screening and risk-of-bias methods before examining results. Protocol registration depends on the topic and registry requirements.

Search and screening

Record reproducible search strings, execution dates and databases. Deduplicate records, screen titles and abstracts, then assess full texts against predefined criteria. Document reasons for full-text exclusion.

Extraction and appraisal

Record design, sample, instruments, effect estimates and limitations. Reporting quality and risk of bias are distinct. Select appraisal tools suitable for the study design. Quantitative synthesis requires a defensible comparison of questions and methods.

Reporting

PRISMA is reporting guidance, not a quality certificate or a replacement for review methods. Report the flow diagram, full search strategies, study characteristics and limitations. Keep conclusions within the evidence.

Choose the review type

Systematic, scoping and narrative reviews have different purposes and methods. Match the question to evidence volume and team resources before starting. Mapping concepts differs from estimating an intervention effect; do not select the label afterward merely for appeal.

Check extraction and synthesis

Pilot the extraction form and define its fields. Explain conflict resolution and team roles in screening and extraction. Check units, direction and design before combining estimates. The availability of meta-analysis software does not justify pooling every study.

Preserve the review record

Retain the protocol, full searches, flow diagram, study table, bias assessment and synthesis rationale. Record update dates and added or removed studies. Explain the consequences of language or full-text restrictions.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

For a fictional active-learning review, define the question and eligibility before a reproducible search. Illustrative accounting: 120 records, 20 duplicates, 100 screened, 15 full texts assessed, five studies included and ten full-text exclusions with reasons. Replace these synthetic counts with actual records and distinguish record, report and study: one study can have multiple reports. PRISMA guides reporting; using its flow diagram alone does not validate searching, eligibility or risk-of-bias assessment.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
ProtocolQuestion and eligibility before searchAre changes dated?
SearchFull query, interface and dateCan a colleague repeat it?
Screening100 illustrative recordsAre disagreements and exclusions logged?
ExtractionStudy ID and linked reportsIs double counting avoided?
SynthesisMethod suited to heterogeneityAre bias and limits reflected?

Exercise output: Deliver the protocol, search log, reconciled flow and extraction table.
outcomes: Deliver the protocol, search log, reconciled flow and extraction table.

en.title: Journal submission and reviewer-response checklist
en.desc: Check journal fit, prepare submission files and declarations, respond to each reviewer comment and inspect the final article proof.
en.body:
Choose a journal

Verify scope, audience, article types, data policy and charges on the journal’s official website. Check indexing in the relevant official database. A familiar name or logo does not establish legitimacy.

Prepare the submission

Prepare the manuscript, tables, high-quality figures, cover letter and required statements. Remove identifying information where anonymous review requires it. Obtain all authors’ approval before submission.

Respond point by point

Address each comment separately and give the page and line of each change. If a suggestion cannot be followed, explain the scientific reason. Use a respectful tone and evidence rather than defensive language.

After acceptance

Check proofs for names, numbers, symbols and citations. Review licensing and access terms. Editors control acceptance and review timing; consultation services cannot guarantee either.

An evidence-based response example

Teaching template: Comment 2 asks how the sample was selected. Response: eligibility and recruitment details were added to Methods, page [x], line [y], and generalizability limits were explained in Discussion. These are placeholders. If a change is not made, explain the scientific reason and supporting evidence.

Anonymous files and versions

Check document properties, acknowledgments, repository links and filenames under the journal’s review policy. Do not remove essential scientific information without justification. Preserve the clean and tracked versions requested by the submission system.

Respond constructively to rejection

Distinguish scope, methods and reporting issues in the decision. Recheck the next journal’s instructions and relevant papers. Reformatting alone cannot resolve a design problem; retain submission versions and respect simultaneous-submission rules.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Compare three hypothetical outlets by scope, article type, preprint policy, current fees, licence, required indexing and author instructions. A name or an intermediary’s claim is insufficient: check the publisher and the relevant official index. Payment requests and guaranteed acceptance are not credibility evidence. Establish other-submission status and coauthor approval before submission. A reviewer response identifies actions or reasoned disagreement and exact change locations; claiming an unmade correction creates another problem.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
FitArticle type and audienceIs it actually within scope?
CredibilityPublisher and official indexAre claims independently checked?
TermsFees, licence and preprintsAre current conditions clear?
SubmissionAuthor approval and submission statusAre statements accurate?
ResponseComment, action, location and versionIs the change actually present?

Exercise output: Prepare an outlet comparison, submission record and response matrix.
outcomes: Prepare an outlet comparison, submission record and response matrix.

en.title: Research data management and reproducibility
en.desc: Build a data dictionary, document cleaning and changes, protect confidential information and preserve code and analysis environments for review.
en.body:
Data dictionary

Define variable names, meaning, units, types, valid ranges and missing-value codes. Separate participant identities from research identifiers. Record transformations and preserve an unchanged raw-data copy.

Cleaning and quality control

Check ranges, duplicate records and inconsistencies. Excluding outliers or imputing missing data requires methodological justification. Report sample counts through cleaning stages so their consequences are visible.

Protection and transfer

Transfer only necessary information and restrict access. Align encryption, backup and retention with institutional requirements. A public messaging channel is not a substitute for an agreed secure process for sensitive data.

Reproducing results

Retain analysis code, software versions and execution order. Data sharing requires consent, permission and regulatory compatibility. If sharing is restricted, document methods and dictionaries or clearly labelled synthetic examples.

A data-dictionary example

For a teaching variable named score, record the construct, instrument, numeric type, permitted range, measurement time, missing code and derivation. Do not impose an invented range on real data. Record formulas and inputs for derived variables.

Versions and change control

Use meaningful filenames and versions. Separate raw and processed data and preserve transformations in code or a decision log. Test backup restoration rather than merely counting copies. Assign folder responsibilities and permissions in collaborative work.

Close the project carefully

An authorized colleague should understand the dataset using the README and dictionary. Retention or deletion follows institutional rules, consent and project agreements rather than a universal period. Match publication availability statements to actual releases and permissions.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

In the fictional dictionary, score is numeric, measured in points, with a teaching range of 0–100 and blank missingness. A value −99 used as a documented missing code must not enter the mean, but replacing it without consulting the dictionary is also wrong. Preserve raw data and encode transformations. Separate linkage IDs from personal identifiers and restrict access in real projects. Retention follows consent, contracts and institutional rules rather than one period for all research.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
Variablescore, points and measurement timeIs the actual definition documented?
MissingnessDocumented code, not analyst assumptionIs conversion correct before calculation?
TransformCode from raw to processedAre changes counted?
AccessResearch ID separate from identityAre permissions and controls adequate?
PreservationVersions, backup and restoration testDoes retention match project policy?

Exercise output: Produce a dictionary, cleaning log and access/retention record.
outcomes: Produce a dictionary, cleaning log and access/retention record.

en.title: AI in research: verification, responsibility and disclosure
en.desc: Use AI responsibly in research: verify sources and calculations, protect confidential information and disclose use under institution and journal policies.
en.body:
Appropriate assistance

Treat brainstorming, code explanations and readability suggestions as proposals to evaluate. Independently verify generated citations, quotations and calculations at original sources or tools. A language model is not an authoritative factual database.

Protect information

Do not upload identifiable participant data, confidential peer-review text or restricted documents without authorization. Review each service’s retention and data-use policy before uploading material.

Responsibility and disclosure

Under ICMJE guidance, AI tools do not meet authorship accountability requirements. Follow institutional or journal policy for disclosure of tools, purpose and affected sections; policies differ between disciplines.

Final verification

Independently check results and references, assess possible bias and keep a record of tool use. No automated detector score alone conclusively establishes text provenance or misconduct.

Maintain a usage record

Record tool and version when available, date, task, permitted input and verification method. Identify assisted passages, code or calculations and who checked them. This record supports review of institutional and journal disclosure requirements.

Verify references and code independently

Locate suggested titles or DOIs on the publisher or repository and match authors and the actual supporting passage. Link resolution alone does not establish correct attribution. Test code on controlled inputs and known-answer cases; successful execution is not scientific validation.

Match use to sensitivity

Public permitted data, unpublished documents and identifiable data need different decisions. Use only necessary information and check actual service terms and project permissions. If permitted use is unclear, consult the responsible institution rather than assuming confidentiality.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

In the exercise an AI tool suggests a plausible but nonexistent reference. Check title, authors and DOI against the original record; if the document cannot be verified, do not present it as a valid source. Disclose actual assistance, scope and human checking under the outlet policy. Do not upload confidential data, restricted manuscripts or participant responses to external tools without permission. Tool output is neither specialist approval nor an accountable author. Record version and date to assess later changes.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
TaskDefined coding or writing assistanceDoes policy permit this use?
SourceNonexistent suggested referenceHas the original been checked?
InputSynthetic instead of confidential dataIs transfer authorized?
ReviewLogic, numbers and attributionCan authors explain the result?
DisclosureTool, version, role and human checksDoes it match actual work?

Exercise output: Keep an AI-use log and source/input checks with the draft.
worksheet: Tool, version, role and human checks
outcomes: Keep an AI-use log and source/input checks with the draft.

en.title: Reproducible literature searching: concepts, databases and logs
en.desc: Build a research search using concepts, synonyms, Boolean logic and suitable databases; preserve a clear search log and manage records without losing provenance.
en.body:
Start with the evidence you need

Specify whether the question concerns experiences, associations, interventions or methods. Split it into a few concepts and list synonyms, variant spellings and disciplinary terms. Translating a local-language title word for word rarely produces a sufficient search.

Teaching example: for active learning and student engagement, create a teaching-method block and an engagement block. Add population or outcome restrictions only after testing whether they remove relevant evidence. This example is not a validated search strategy.

Translate the strategy for each database

OR commonly combines synonyms and AND joins concepts, but phrase searching, truncation and field tags differ between interfaces. Consult the database’s own guide. In PubMed, review MeSH and automatic term mapping instead of assuming that an exact phrase and a mapped query behave identically.

Use more than one discovery route

Match the database to the discipline and document type. A library catalog such as HOLLIS can help discover books and other materials, but discovery does not grant access to every licensed item. Inspect references and forward citations of key studies. A broad search engine does not establish comprehensive disciplinary coverage.

Preserve the search history

Record database, interface, execution date, full query, limits and result count. Keep the original export; deduplicate with identifiers and title checks rather than an opaque deletion rule. For systematic reviews, also preserve screening decisions and reasons for full-text exclusions. A later rerun may produce different counts because database coverage changes.

Test and deliver the strategy

Check whether known relevant studies are retrieved and inspect where irrelevant results originate. A specialist librarian can help review the strategy. Deliver the search log, original records, deduplication rules and update date. Describe coverage and limitations instead of claiming an unexplained complete search.

Practical research checklist

  • Define the question and eligibility rules.
  • Test syntax separately in every interface.
  • Preserve exports and query versions.
  • Keep discovery separate from study appraisal.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Break the fictional academic-support question into student population, support and engagement blocks. Combine synonyms within blocks with OR and concepts with AND. Translate syntax and fields for each database; the same pasted query can behave differently across interfaces. Test known relevant papers to detect an overly restrictive strategy and log revisions. General web search helps discovery but alone is not a complete systematic-review strategy. Preserve exports and distinguish discovery from reading and appraisal.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
Blockstudent OR undergraduateAre local terms and synonyms considered?
Combinationpopulation AND support AND engagementAre logic and parentheses correct?
DatabaseName, interface and fieldsIs syntax interface-specific?
CheckKnown relevant studyDoes the query retrieve it?
LogDate, query, count and exportIs it repeatable and auditable?

Exercise output: Prepare a multi-database search log and a read-source matrix.
worksheet: Are local terms and synonyms considered?
outcomes: Prepare a multi-database search log and a read-source matrix.

en.title: Choosing a research design: questions, data and methods
en.desc: Align descriptive, predictive or causal aims with study design, measurement and the unit of analysis; document feasibility and bias before collecting data.
en.body:
Different questions require different evidence

Describing a situation, predicting an outcome and estimating an intervention effect are different aims. A highly accurate predictor does not automatically identify causal effects. Write down the purpose, target population and outcome before choosing a statistical package.

Specify the unit and dependencies

Cross-sectional, longitudinal, experimental, qualitative and mixed-method designs have distinct requirements. State whether the unit is a person, class, organization, interview or repeated observation. Repeated measurements and clustered samples cannot simply be treated as independent observations; collection and analysis should respect these dependencies.

Connect concepts to measurements

Separate a theoretical construct from the instrument used to measure it. Document definitions, timing, units, ranges and model roles. Reliability alone does not establish construct validity. A translated instrument also needs appropriate linguistic and cultural assessment.

Check feasibility and bias

Review actual sample access, recruitment time, resources, permissions, computing needs and attrition. Describe differences between accessible participants and the target population. Maintain a risk table with the issue, consequence, mitigation and remaining limitation.

Create a defensible design record

Map each question to the required data, collection procedure, analysis, key assumption and output. Revise questions lacking suitable evidence or methods. A pilot can expose recording and workflow problems, but does not replace the main design. Include unresolved decisions so that a supervisor can review them before collection begins.

Practical research checklist

  • Distinguish descriptive, predictive and causal goals.
  • Define the unit and dependencies.
  • Check construct and measurement alignment.
  • Document permissions, resources and limitations.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Similar questions need different designs. “Who uses support?” is descriptive; “Does support increase engagement?” needs an intervention or defensible causal strategy. Cross-sectional data leave temporal order and self-selection unresolved. If a causal design is infeasible, narrow the question and title to an estimable association. A mixed-methods project specifies where and why the components integrate; adding a few interviews alone does not create a coherent mixed-methods design.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
QuestionDescription, association or effect?Is the claim type explicit?
TimeBefore and after exposureIs temporal order known?
SelectionVolunteers or probability sampleIs selection bias assessed?
MeasurementComparable definitions across groupsIs comparison valid?
IntegrationDefined quantitative and qualitative rolesHow do outputs answer one question?

Exercise output: Create a design rationale and claim/data/assumption matrix.
worksheet: How do outputs answer one question?
outcomes: Create a design rationale and claim/data/assumption matrix.

en.title: Preregistration and analysis plans: decisions before results
en.desc: Preregister questions, outcomes, sampling and confirmatory analyses; disclose prior data access, changes and exploratory work with a transparent decision record.
en.body:
Why record decisions in advance?

Preregistration makes planned decisions distinguishable from choices informed by results. It supports transparency rather than certifying study quality. Exploratory work remains valuable when it is clearly identified instead of presented as a prespecified confirmation.

Specify actionable details

Include questions, hypotheses, primary outcomes, measurement, population, sampling, sample-size justification, stopping rules, exclusions, missing-data handling and the main model. Explain multiple-testing decisions when appropriate. Saying that a suitable test will be selected leaves the critical choice undocumented.

Be candid about existing data

For secondary data or a late registration, record which information and outcomes were already known and when they were accessed. Do not change the original date or describe a plan made after inspecting outcomes as the initial plan.

Changes and registry selection

A design problem or a better method may justify a change. Preserve the original version, date, rationale and implications; label additional analyses. Choose a registry appropriate to the discipline and institutional requirements, and check its current service conditions. Review protocols and trial registrations have different purposes.

Prepare an auditable package

Deliver the readable analysis plan, registration identifier, amendments and a planned-versus-executed table. Adapt the downloadable toolkit template to the study. Preregistration does not replace ethics review, consent or other mandatory study registration.

Practical research checklist

  • Define primary outcomes and models in advance.
  • Disclose prior access to data.
  • Retain dated and justified amendments.
  • Label exploratory analyses clearly.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

The teaching plan identifies score as the primary outcome, one semester as the window and a defined planned model. A later-discovered variable is exploratory and described in a dated amendment, not silently inserted into the old plan. New, secondary and qualitative data need different registration choices. Registered Reports are not equivalent to uploading a form. Specify decisions sufficiently to distinguish prospective commitments from choices made after viewing data.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
QuestionDefined association, not desired resultAre hypothesis and units clear?
Prior accessWhich data/outputs were seen?Is this disclosed before registration?
PlanOutcome, exclusions, missingness and modelAre ambiguous choices reduced?
AmendmentChange after a new variable is seenAre date, reason and consequence recorded?
ReportPlanned and exploratory separatedDoes it match registration history?

Exercise output: Prepare an assessable plan, prior-access disclosure and deviation log.
worksheet: Change after a new variable is seen
Are date, reason and consequence recorded?
outcomes: Prepare an assessable plan, prior-access disclosure and deviation log.

en.title: Sample size and statistical power: a defensible justification
en.desc: Justify sample size using the primary outcome, study design, plausible effect, power or precision; document attrition, clustering and sensitivity scenarios.
en.body:
Start with the primary analysis

Estimating a proportion, comparing means, fitting regression, cluster sampling and survival analysis have different requirements. A formula for a simple survey is not automatically appropriate for a complex model or a qualitative study. Specify the main outcome and design first.

Choose defensible assumptions

A power calculation needs an appropriate test, target effect, type-I error level, power, sidedness and allocation assumptions. Justify the effect using prior evidence, a meaningful threshold or a scientific scenario. Choosing it only to obtain a cheaper sample is not a scientific rationale.

Consider precision and design

The goal may be a sufficiently precise interval rather than a significance threshold. Repeated measurements, clustering and imbalanced data can require specialist methods or simulation. UCLA’s G*Power examples address particular tests; verify the match to your design independently.

Plan attrition and sensitivity

For n analyzable observations and anticipated attrition r, n/(1−r) is a simple recruitment approximation under explicit assumptions; round upward. Compare plausible effect and attrition scenarios. After observing results, do not substitute observed power for interval estimates or the original design justification.

Report enough to reproduce the calculation

Preserve software and version, test, every input, supporting assumptions and scenario results. Explain for which outcome and assumptions a proposed sample is adequate rather than declaring a universal number. Final study planning requires review of the actual design and resources.

Practical research checklist

  • Match the test to the research design.
  • Justify effect and precision.
  • Account for clustering and attrition.
  • Preserve inputs and sensitivity scenarios.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Suppose an independently justified plan needs 100 analyzable observations and expects 15% attrition. The simple recruitment approximation 100/0.85 rounds up to 118; at 25% attrition it becomes 134. This arithmetic does not justify the initial 100 or account for clustering. Use scenarios to expose risk. If classes or repeated measures are involved, participants are not automatically independent observations. Preserve every calculation input and the effect rationale, not only the software’s final number.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
GoalPower or precision for the main outcomeDoes it match the design?
Analyzable need100 is an exercise assumptionWas the actual need properly calculated?
15% attritionApproximate recruitment 118Is the rate justified?
25% attritionApproximate recruitment 134Is the harder scenario covered?
StructurePossible clusters or repetitionAre independence assumptions defensible?

Exercise output: Save calculation inputs, scenarios and the design rationale.
worksheet: Power or precision for the main outcome
Was the actual need properly calculated?
outcomes: Save calculation inputs, scenarios and the design rationale.

en.title: Effect sizes, confidence intervals and p-values
en.desc: Report magnitude, direction, units and uncertainty alongside significance tests; separate exploratory analyses and avoid treating nonsignificance as proof of no effect.
en.body:
Keep the substantive question visible

Describe how large a difference or association is and what it means for the research question. Report original units, relevant populations and timeframes. Standardized effects can help comparison but may obscure the meaning of the original scale.

Understand what a p-value does not establish

The ASA statement warns against interpreting a p-value alone as the probability that the null hypothesis is true, effect magnitude or scientific importance. Do not reduce research decisions to a threshold. Sample size and design influence the evidence.

Report uncertainty and assumptions

Present the estimate, interval and calculation method. Frequentist coverage concerns the procedure’s repeated-sampling behavior, rather than a probability assigned to a fixed parameter after the interval is observed. Model assumptions, dependence, selection bias and missingness can limit interpretation.

Address multiple analyses

Separate primary confirmatory outcomes from exploratory analyses and explain multiplicity handling. A nonsignificant finding alone demonstrates neither equivalence nor absence of an effect. Equivalence requires its own question, margin and suitable design.

A transparent reporting template

Teaching template: estimated difference [value and units], interval [lower, upper], method [model and settings], key limitation [limitation]. These placeholders are not actual results. Add the analytical sample and sensitivity to important decisions; an isolated number is insufficient.

Practical research checklist

  • State effect, direction and units.
  • Report the interval and method.
  • Include all primary analyses.
  • Keep conclusions within design and evidence.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

A teaching mean difference of 2 points with CI95=[−1,5] leaves a small negative and a larger positive effect compatible with the model. It proves neither no effect nor practical usefulness. Report units, interval method and design. If 4 points was the prespecified practical threshold, this interval remains uncertain relative to it. Distinguish raw and standardized effects and explain the denominator and target population rather than treating all effect sizes as interchangeable.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
EstimateHypothetical 2 pointsAre units and direction clear?
CI95Illustrative [−1,5]Are method and assumptions suitable?
Importance4 is only a teaching thresholdWas the actual threshold justified prospectively?
InterpretationUncertainty remainsIs p distinct from size and precision?
ReportRaw, standardized and limitsIs the standardizing denominator defined?

Exercise output: Write an estimate/interval/unit/importance-threshold table.
worksheet: Was the actual threshold justified prospectively?
Is p distinct from size and precision?

en.title: Missing data and sensitivity analysis
en.desc: Inspect missingness patterns, distinguish assumptions from evidence and justify complete-case or imputation methods; report analytical samples and sensitivity transparently.
en.body:
Describe the pattern first

Summarize missing values by variable and group. Distinguish zero, unknown, not applicable and recording failures. Preserve known reasons and improve collection where missingness is preventable.

Treat mechanisms as assumptions

MCAR, MAR and MNAR concern relationships between missingness and observed or unobserved information. A pattern or test cannot establish all these assumptions. Use subject knowledge, collection procedures and sensitivity analyses.

Avoid automatic deletion or mean replacement

Complete-case analysis changes the analytical sample and may be biased under some mechanisms. Mean replacement commonly distorts variability and relationships. Neither should be selected by default without checking design and analytical goals.

Multiple imputation requires a full workflow

The R package mice creates multiple imputed datasets; analyze and pool them appropriately. Check variable types, temporal or clustered structure, auxiliary information, diagnostics and plausible imputed values. Do not present imputed values as actually measured observations.

Report decisions and their consequences

Document sample changes, patterns, assumptions, methods and settings; compare plausible alternatives. Explain material dependence of conclusions on these decisions. A missingness percentage alone does not provide a universal rule for selecting the method.

Practical research checklist

  • Separate missing codes from zero and inapplicability.
  • Justify mechanisms and methods.
  • Document analysis and pooling.
  • Report sample changes and sensitivity.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

In the fictional sample, 12 of 100 outcomes are missing and nine missing cases have low baseline scores. This pattern warrants investigation but alone establishes neither MAR nor MNAR. Count missingness by variable and time and distinguish known reasons from guesses. Do not default to complete-case analysis or mean substitution without rationale. If multiple imputation is chosen, document its model, auxiliary variables, number of datasets and pooling, and assess compatibility with the design and sensitivity to untestable assumptions.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
Count12 of 100 in the exampleLogged by variable and time?
ReasonKnown, unknown or hypothesizedAre guesses labeled?
AssumptionDefensible missingness mechanismAre evidence and limits stated?
MethodJustified deletion or imputationCompatible with design and analysis?
SensitivityDefensible alternative assumptionAre changes in results reported?

Exercise output: Prepare a missingness map, method rationale and sensitivity table.
outcomes: Prepare a missingness map, method rationale and sensitivity table.

en.title: Qualitative research: interviews, coding and interpretation
en.desc: Connect qualitative questions to sampling, researcher reflexivity and documented interpretation; choose reporting guidance that fits the specific methodology.
en.body:
Choose a coherent approach

Qualitative work investigates meaning, experience and processes, but not through one universal method. Explain the epistemological position and analytical approach. Thematic analysis, grounded theory and phenomenology carry different commitments.

Explain sampling and positionality

Document why people or settings were selected and describe access limitations. Interview counts are not governed by a universal number. Preserve reflexive notes about researcher assumptions and relationships with participants.

Preserve context in collection

Pilot open questions and follow-up prompts. Establish appropriate arrangements for recording, quotations and retention. Document transcription and translation choices that affect meaning and remove identifying details appropriately.

Make interpretation traceable

Connect codes, extracts, analytical notes and category revisions. Software organizes materials but does not establish the validity of an interpretation. Use coder agreement or saturation only when coherent with the chosen approach and clearly defined.

Report within methodological limits

COREQ addresses reporting interviews and focus groups; other methods may need other guidance. Quotations should support interpretation and respect privacy. Examine contradictory cases and alternatives, and do not infer statistical generalizability automatically from purposive sampling.

Practical research checklist

  • Explain the methodological approach.
  • Document sampling and researcher role.
  • Connect codes, evidence and interpretations.
  • Use appropriate reporting guidance.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

For a fictional support-experience study, “Describe a recent situation when seeking help was easy or difficult” is less leading than “Why is university support poor?” The synthetic excerpt “I did not know whom to ask” may receive the initial code access-route uncertainty; one code is not a final theme. Record context, researcher position, sampling and interpretive memos. Saturation or adequacy criteria must fit the actual methodological approach rather than a universal interview number.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
PromptExperience without a forced answerCompatible with the approach?
SampleRelevant diversity and ethical accessIs selection explained?
CodeAccess-route uncertainty in synthetic textIs it grounded in context?
InterpretationComparison and reflexive memoAre contrasts and counterexamples considered?
ReportPermitted non-identifying excerptsAre consent and COREQ applicability assessed?

Exercise output: Create an interview guide, interpretation log and permitted coding example.
worksheet: Are consent and COREQ applicability assessed?
outcomes: Create an interview guide, interpretation log and permitted coding example.

en.title: Survey design: questions, piloting and response quality
en.desc: Translate constructs into clear questions and answer scales; test wording, order, burden and language equivalence before running the final questionnaire.
en.body:
Define constructs and use

Specify the construct or behavior, timeframe and intended analysis. Existing instruments need appropriate permissions and relevant measurement evidence. A longer questionnaire is not necessarily a better one.

Avoid ambiguous wording

Ask one interpretable question at a time. Combining instructor quality and facilities in one item prevents separate interpretation. Avoid leading terms, unsupported assumptions and unfamiliar jargon. Match answer options to the concept and respondent recall.

Review order and administration

Question order, mode and option presentation can influence responses. Randomization is not suitable for every naturally ordered scale. Test mobile display, completion time, branching and withdrawal.

Use cognitive testing and a pilot

Ask potential respondents how they interpret items and choose answers. Complement this with a small workflow pilot for missingness, timing and interface errors. Assess semantic and cultural equivalence in multilingual instruments; back-translation alone is not sufficient.

Preserve the actual questionnaire

Keep wording, options, order, version date, instructions, branching and pilot changes. Define response-rate denominators and do not describe a convenience sample as representative of all students. Deliver a construct-to-item-to-analysis mapping.

Practical research checklist

  • Give each item an explicit purpose.
  • Clarify timeframes and options.
  • Document pilots and translation review.
  • Preserve the administered version.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

“Are you satisfied with the instructor and facilities?” combines two concepts; a respondent may be satisfied with one and not the other. Split it into suitable items with explicit timeframes and options. For a behaviour, “How many times in the last four weeks…” can be clearer than “usually,” if recall is feasible. Cognitive interviews examine interpretation, while a pilot checks flow, timing and form errors. Neither alone establishes construct validity. Preserve the version actually administered.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
ConstructTeaching satisfaction separate from facilitiesOne concept per item?
TimeframeFour weeks in the behaviour exampleCompatible with recall?
OptionsRange and non-applicability where justifiedDo real answers fit?
PilotMeaning, branching and mobile displayAre changes logged?
VersionActual wording and orderDoes analysis use this version?

Exercise output: Create a construct/item map, pilot record and final questionnaire version.
worksheet: Four weeks in the behaviour example
outcomes: Create a construct/item map, pilot record and final questionnaire version.

en.title: Association and causal inference: questions and assumptions
en.desc: Separate association, prediction and causal effects; define the intervention, timing, confounders and identification assumptions before interpreting a model causally.
en.body:
Define a meaningful contrast

Specify the intervention, population, comparison and outcome time. An association between attendance and grades differs from the effect of a defined attendance program. Without a clear contrast, a claim that X affects Y is underspecified.

Consider time and variable roles

Record when exposure, covariates and outcomes occur. Confounders, mediators and selection variables have different roles. Adjusting for every available variable may introduce bias; justify the set using subject knowledge and explicit assumptions.

Make assumptions reviewable

Causal diagrams can expose assumptions and bias paths but cannot establish that those assumptions are true. Appropriate methods require attention to exchangeability, intervention consistency and comparison support. Some identifying assumptions cannot be verified from the observed dataset alone.

Design matters more than a coefficient

Randomization helps control some confounding when implemented appropriately; attrition, adherence and measurement still matter. Observational inference needs a defensible design and assumptions. Significance or predictive accuracy alone is insufficient for a causal claim.

Report limitations and sensitivity

Describe the target effect, identification strategy, adjustment choices and sensitivity to assumptions. Use association language when the design supports only association. Educational guidance cannot substitute for specialist review of the actual study.

Practical research checklist

  • Define intervention, population and timing.
  • Justify covariate roles.
  • Disclose identification assumptions and bias.
  • Match claims to the design.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Prior motivation may affect both support use and later participation in an observational example, so their association need not be the support effect. A post-treatment variable may be a mediator, and adjusting for it can change the estimand. Select adjustment using causal assumptions and measurement timing rather than each covariate’s p-value. Define the intervention, population and time, and explain exchangeability, overlap and consistency. Data alone cannot fully prove these assumptions.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
TargetEffect of a defined interventionDistinct from descriptive association?
TimingPrior motivation and later outcomeIs temporal order credible?
AdjustmentConfounders under a causal modelAre mediators/colliders handled deliberately?
CoverageComparable groupsAre overlap and selection assessed?
SensitivityUnmeasured confoundingAre claims explicitly limited?

Exercise output: Document the estimand, causal assumptions and adjustment rationale.
outcomes: Document the estimand, causal assumptions and adjustment rationale.

en.title: Reproducible notebooks: Jupyter, R and execution environments
en.desc: Combine scientific explanation with code; control hidden state, dependencies, data paths and outputs so a colleague can rerun the analytical workflow.
en.body:
Write an analytical narrative

Explain the purpose, data provenance, transformations, assumptions and interpretation alongside the code. Jupyter combines text, code and outputs; an R reporting workflow should preserve the same traceable reasoning.

Eliminate hidden session state

Out-of-order cells can reuse stale variables or session-dependent results. Restart the environment and run every step in order. Stored output may belong to an older code version, so prepare a clean execution before publishing.

Record inputs and environment

Document language and package versions, environment setup, random seeds and data locations. A fixed seed alone does not guarantee identical behavior across all hardware. Provide permitted data or clearly labeled teaching data and explain access restrictions. Keep credentials and confidential data out of repositories.

Organize and check the workflow

Move reusable logic into functions and add meaningful checks for ranges, record counts and known answers. Use documented relative paths. Separate raw data, processed data and outputs and preserve transformation decisions.

Deliver a rerunnable package

Include a README, execution command, environment description, sample or accessible inputs, executed notebook and expected outputs. A colleague should not need undocumented steps. HTML and PDF aid reading but do not replace the code and environment needed for rerunning.

Practical research checklist

  • Complete a clean ordered run.
  • Record versions and setup.
  • Explain inputs, outputs and provenance.
  • Include documentation and scientific checks.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

A notebook can show attractive output while relying on a variable created only in an earlier session. Restart the kernel and execute all cells in order: an undefined name reveals a state or ordering problem. Old displayed output is not reproduction evidence. Record data, environment, relevant random seeds and execution commands; reconcile figures and text against fresh output. Successful execution on one machine does not guarantee identical behaviour on every system.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
Clean startFresh kernel and cleared outputsAny hidden state?
OrderRun all cells from the topIndependent of prior clicks?
EnvironmentLibrary and data versionsAre setup commands explicit?
RandomnessSeed and system limitsAre determinism claims justified?
DeliveryFresh output and execution logDo document numbers agree?

Exercise output: Keep the clean-run notebook, environment and execution log.
worksheet: Run all cells from the top
outcomes: Keep the clean-run notebook, environment and execution log.

en.title: FAIR research data: metadata, licensing and reuse
en.desc: Document data with metadata, a README, persistent identifiers and access conditions; distinguish FAIR practice from unrestricted sharing or simply uploading a file.
en.body:
What FAIR aims to improve

Findability, accessibility, interoperability and reuse involve more than offering a download. Sensitive data may require authorization, with restrictions and request procedures explained. FAIR does not imply unrestricted openness.

Make documentation useful

Record the collection title and version, contact, permitted context, methods, units, missing-value codes and limitations. A README supports human understanding while structured metadata supports discovery. Undefined columns and unexplained provenance undermine reuse.

Check rights before release

Review ownership, consent, project obligations and re-identification risks. Data, code, figures and text can have different licensing conditions. Do not assign a license to materials you lack the right to release; controlled access or documentation-only sharing may be appropriate.

Choose a repository and version

Compare disciplinary and institutional repositories for formats, size, preservation, service terms and confidentiality. A DOI supports citation and discovery, not scientific validation. Preserve release versions and changes; a mutable folder link does not identify a stable release.

Assemble a coherent package

Connect permitted data, dictionary, README, processing methods, code where appropriate and an accurate availability statement. Specify location, version and restrictions. Explain valid non-sharing reasons and lawful access routes; label synthetic examples explicitly.

Practical research checklist

  • Define variables and provenance.
  • Check rights and access conditions.
  • Specify identifier and release version.
  • Match availability statements to actual files.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Sensitive interview data can become more FAIR without opening every transcript. The teaching record exposes title, methods, dictionary and access-request conditions while permitted text remains controlled. Persistent identifiers, metadata standards and explicit permissions help, but consent and identification risk still govern release. This matrix identifies package gaps; it is neither official FAIR certification nor publication permission. Public data also need version and citation instructions.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
FindablePublic record and stable identifierEnough discovery metadata?
AccessiblePermitted request processAre conditions and responsibility clear?
InteroperableSuitable units and standard codesCan users interpret variables?
ReusableRights, provenance and qualityAre use limits stated?
ProtectionControlled sensitive dataIs openness distinguished from permission?

Exercise output: Prepare metadata, access conditions and a permitted reuse package.
outcomes: Prepare metadata, access conditions and a permitted reuse package.

en.title: Open access and publishing rights: versions and repositories
en.desc: Check open-access routes, article versions, embargoes, licenses and costs in official policies; free reading does not imply unrestricted reuse or universal repository eligibility.
en.body:
Separate access from reuse

Free reading does not automatically permit translation, figure reuse or commercial redistribution. Check the actual license and agreement. Preprints, accepted manuscripts and publisher versions can have different conditions.

Compare routes and costs

Consider open-access journal publication and depositing an allowed version in a repository. Some journals charge and others do not; openness alone establishes neither price nor quality. University publisher agreements, including Oxford’s arrangements, do not automatically cover all researchers.

Check repository eligibility

Institutional repositories such as Apollo and OpenUCT preserve their communities’ outputs. Review membership, accepted versions, file formats and embargo rules. Reading a repository’s contents does not confer the right to deposit there.

Evaluate the publication venue

Verify publisher identity, peer review, fees, contact details and correction policies. DOAJ helps discover open-access journals but does not replace assessment of scientific fit. Familiar branding and rapid acceptance promises are insufficient evidence of trustworthiness.

Keep a rights record

Preserve the accepted version, agreement, license, deposit date, funding statement and publication identifier. Verify the terms for each reused figure or file. Clearly identify versions and peer-review status when listing your work.

Practical research checklist

  • Identify the version and license.
  • Check fees and possible support.
  • Verify repository deposit conditions.
  • Describe review status accurately.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

For the fictional paper, compare repository access to an accepted manuscript with open access to the publisher version. Free reading does not imply no author charge, and viewing a free file does not establish reuse permission. Check current fees and waivers with the official outlet; this site promises neither fixed prices nor indexing. A preprint usually precedes journal review and needs an accurate status in citations and CVs. Review agreements, funder conditions and third-party rights.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
VersionAAM or VoRCorrectly labeled?
CostCurrent charge and waiver conditionsChecked with the publisher?
LicenceReading versus reuseAre permissions explicit?
PreprintClear review statusNot mislabeled peer-reviewed?
DepositFunder, agreement and repositoryAre timing and permissions compatible?

Exercise output: Create an access-route, cost, rights and version-status comparison.
outcomes: Create an access-route, cost, rights and version-status comparison.

en.title: ORCID, DOI and researcher identity
en.desc: Distinguish researcher identifiers from output identifiers; reconcile names, authors, versions and affiliations, and avoid treating an identifier as proof of research quality.
en.body:
Different identifiers serve different entities

ORCID helps distinguish researchers with similar names. A DOI identifies a research output or record; it is not a person identifier. A thesis and its subsequent article may be separate records.

Verify the record

Check author order, title, date, document type and version against the original source. ORCID visibility controls and imported records do not establish that every listed work is peer reviewed. Align affiliations with the actual work and venue requirements.

Resolve and compare DOIs

Copy the identifier from the publisher or repository and follow doi.org. Crossref and DataCite provide metadata for research outputs. Successful resolution alone is insufficient: the title and authors must match the intended reference.

Handle multilingual and duplicate names

Keep necessary Persian, Arabic and Latin name variants consistent. Automatic profiles can merge different people or split one researcher’s works. Correct records in the responsible service and check your reference library again after merging duplicates.

Interpret metrics carefully

Identifiers support linking and citation, not independent quality certification. Record database coverage and extraction dates when reporting metrics. The toolkit’s DOI link builder formats a link; it does not verify that the work exists or is correct.

Practical research checklist

  • Separate person and output identifiers.
  • Match metadata to the original.
  • Specify version and relevant affiliation.
  • Check duplicate and mistaken identities.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

ORCID distinguishes a researcher from namesakes; a DOI identifies a research object. Neither alone validates quality. Record the first and corrected dataset versions and explain their relationship under the repository’s versioning policy. Check a displayed DOI against destination title and authors. This site’s DOI link builder checks syntax, not existence or correctness. Copy identifiers from the authoritative record rather than inventing them.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
PersonOwner-confirmed ORCIDAre namesakes resolved?
ObjectDOI from the authoritative recordDo title and authors match?
VersionInitial and corrected dataAre version relationships clear?
CitationThe version actually usedDoes the identifier resolve to it?
QualitySeparate methodological assessmentIs identity distinct from validity?

en.title: Research reporting guidelines: PRISMA, CONSORT and COREQ
en.desc: Choose reporting guidance by study design; check PRISMA 2020, CONSORT and SPIRIT 2025, qualitative guidance and journal-specific requirements.
en.body:
Reporting is not methodological certification

A checklist helps prevent omissions but cannot repair an invalid study. Read it during planning and record where each applicable item is addressed. A tick without supporting information is not transparent reporting.

Match design and version

Review PRISMA 2020 for systematic reviews, CONSORT for randomized trial reports and SPIRIT for related protocols. Official sources include the 2025 CONSORT and SPIRIT updates. Use EQUATOR to locate suitable guidance for observational, qualitative, diagnostic and other designs.

Check extensions and scope

Cluster, pilot and specialized studies may require extensions. A familiar acronym is insufficient. COREQ targets interviews and focus groups rather than every qualitative method.

Use a coverage table

Record the item, manuscript location and status or explanation. Explain inapplicable items; add design-appropriate flow diagrams, protocols, search strategies and supplements. Reconcile their counts with the reported sample.

Prepare for submission

Keep the version, access date, completed checklist and journal requirements. Manage differences when a journal specifies another version. Authors must ensure tables and declarations reflect what was actually done.

Practical research checklist

  • Match guidance to the design.
  • Select the appropriate version and extension.
  • Provide locations or non-applicability reasons.
  • Reconcile checklists, diagrams and manuscript.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

Start with the study type: a trial report, protocol, review and qualitative interview study have different needs. Map each applicable item to evidence in text or appendices and label incomplete or non-applicable items with reasons. A standard name without a version, or several unrelated checklists, adds little. Separate guides cover CONSORT/SPIRIT 2025 and PRISMA-LSR 2024. Recheck official listings, explanatory documents and outlet rules before submission.

Worked case and implementation decisions
StageTeaching exampleVerification question
DesignActual study typeIs guidance applicable?
VersionSpecific year and extensionIs official status checked?
ItemEvidence in section/appendixMore than an unsupported tick?
GapExplanation and correctionIs design deficiency disclosed?
SubmissionMatrix and outlet requirementDoes the final version match?

Exercise output: Build a guideline/version/evidence matrix with non-applicability reasons.
outcomes: Build a guideline/version/evidence matrix with non-applicability reasons.

en.title: Research grant planning: fit, budget and timeline
en.desc: Match the idea to the current funding call and eligibility rules; prepare coherent aims, resources, justified budgets, data plans and internal submission deadlines.
en.body:
Read the opportunity before the form

Check scope, applicant type, country or institution eligibility, allowable costs and deadline in the current call. NIH guidance illustrates a process; it does not establish eligibility for every student or availability of a particular opportunity.

Connect aims to feasibility

Explain the question, significance, contribution and methods for each aim. Present preliminary evidence, facilities and collaborator roles honestly. Expected future findings are not completed results.

Build the budget from activities

Connect each activity to resources, time and justified costs. Institutional rules and the call govern rates, purchases, travel, software and data-management costs. Record currency, estimate date and assumptions; this guide does not provide current rates.

Work backward from deadlines

Accounts, organizational authorization, letters, CVs, data plans and internal review may require separate lead times. Allow time for revisions and submission problems. Distinguish institutional deadlines and portal time zones from the final deadline.

Review a coherent application

Locate evidence for each review criterion and reconcile title, aims, budget, schedule, team and data planning. Preserve the final version, approvals and submission receipt. Funding decisions depend on the actual opportunity and competition and cannot be guaranteed.

Practical research checklist

  • Check current eligibility.
  • Link aims, methods and resources.
  • Justify costs and assumptions.
  • Record internal deadlines and receipt.

Worked case and implementation decisions

The following is a fictional teaching case. Do not use its numbers or wording as actual study findings.

The fictional grant has work packages for measurement and permissions, authorized collection, and analysis/publication. Link costs to activities and outputs; this guide supplies no actual tariff. Delayed approval may trigger a permitted secondary-data contingency, but question/design changes still need approval. Read the call’s eligibility, allowable costs and impact requirements. “Definitely solving a global problem” is not a substitute for a measurable bounded project contribution.

PackageActivity, owner, output and timingAre dependencies defined?
